preamble: An Act to consolidate and to provide for general rules and principles of evidence for fair trial.

glossary.adhiniyam: The Hindi-derived term used throughout this Act to mean the Act itself -- “Adhiniyam” is simply the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023's word for “this Act”, used the way “Sanhita” is used in the BNSS and BNS.
glossary.conclusive proof: The strongest form of proof recognised by this Adhiniyam: when a fact is declared conclusive proof of another under section 2(1)(b), the Court must treat the second fact as proved the moment the first is proved, and no evidence disproving it may even be admitted -- unlike an ordinary presumption, it cannot be rebutted.
glossary.disproved: A fact is “disproved”, under section 2(1)(c), when the Court either believes it does not exist, or considers its non-existence so probable that a prudent person ought to act on the supposition that it does not exist -- the mirror image of “proved”.
glossary.facts in issue: Facts from which the existence, non-existence, nature or extent of a right, liability or disability asserted or denied in a suit or proceeding necessarily follows -- in essence, the facts the parties actually dispute and which the Court must decide, as opposed to merely “relevant” facts that help prove or disprove them. Defined in section 2(1)(g).
glossary.may presume: One of three defined presumption strengths in section 2(1)(h): where the Adhiniyam says the Court “may presume” a fact, the Court has discretion to either treat it as proved unless disproved, or to instead call for proof -- the weakest and most discretionary of the three presumption types (compare “shall presume” and “conclusive proof”).
glossary.shall presume: The middle tier of the three presumption strengths in section 2(1): where the Adhiniyam directs that the Court “shall presume” a fact, the Court has no discretion -- it must regard the fact as proved unless and until it is disproved by the other side. Unlike “conclusive proof”, this kind of presumption can be rebutted with evidence.
glossary.not proved: A distinct, third status under section 2(1)(i), separate from both “proved” and “disproved”: a fact is “not proved” when the evidence leaves the Court unable to either believe it exists or believe it does not -- the position of genuine uncertainty.
glossary.res gestae: A common-law Latin label (not itself used in the Adhiniyam's text) traditionally applied to the doctrine now codified in section 4: facts so closely connected with a fact in issue as to form part of the same transaction are themselves relevant, regardless of whether they occurred at the same time and place.
glossary.conduct: Under section 6(2), the actions of a party, their agent, or a person whose alleged offence is the subject of the proceeding are relevant if they influence, or are influenced by, a fact in issue or relevant fact. Explanation 1 to section 6 clarifies that mere statements are not “conduct” unless they accompany and explain some other act.
glossary.court: Defined broadly in section 2(1)(a) to include all Judges and Magistrates, and all persons legally authorised to take evidence -- except arbitrators, who are expressly excluded (consistent with section 1(2) taking arbitration proceedings outside this Adhiniyam's scope entirely).
glossary.document: Defined in section 2(1)(d) as any matter expressed, described, or otherwise recorded on any substance by letters, figures, marks, or any other means (or combination of means), intended or usable for recording that matter -- and expressly including electronic and digital records such as emails, server logs, and messages, reflecting this Adhiniyam's modernisation of the old Evidence Act's definition.
glossary.evidence: Defined in section 2(1)(e) to mean and include both oral evidence (statements, including electronic statements, that a witness makes before the Court) and documentary evidence (documents, including electronic or digital records, produced for the Court's inspection).
glossary.fact: Defined in section 2(1)(f) to include any thing, state of things, or relation of things capable of being perceived by the senses, and any mental condition a person is conscious of -- covering both physical, observable facts and internal mental facts like intention or good faith.
glossary.proved: Defined in section 2(1)(j): a fact is “proved” when, after considering the matters before it, the Court either believes it exists, or considers its existence so probable that a prudent person ought to act on the supposition that it exists -- the basic evidentiary threshold applied throughout the Adhiniyam.
glossary.relevant: Defined in section 2(1)(k): a fact is “relevant” to another when it is connected to it in one of the specific ways described in this Adhiniyam's provisions on relevancy of facts (sections 3 onward) -- relevance is not a matter of general logic or common sense alone, but of falling within one of these codified categories of connection.
glossary.conspiracy: An agreement or common design between two or more persons to commit an offence or an actionable wrong. Section 8 makes anything said, done, or written by any one conspirator in reference to their common intention relevant against every other person believed to be part of the conspiracy, even if that person was unaware of the specific act or a stranger to the person who did it.
glossary.state of mind: A person's intention, knowledge, good faith, negligence, rashness, ill-will, or goodwill towards someone -- an internal, mental fact. Section 12 makes facts showing the existence of a relevant state of mind (or of body/bodily feeling) relevant, but Explanation 1 requires the state of mind shown to relate specifically to the matter in question, not merely to a general disposition or character trait.
glossary.admission: A statement -- oral, documentary, or in electronic form -- that suggests an inference as to a fact in issue or relevant fact, made by specified categories of persons under specified circumstances. Section 15 opens the Adhiniyam's dedicated sub-topic on admissions, which governs when such statements can be used as evidence against the person who (or whose privy) made them.

sections.title: Short title, application and commencement
sections.raw_text:
1. (1) This Act may be called the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023.
(2) It applies to all judicial proceedings in or before any Court, including Courts-martial, but not to affidavits presented to any Court or officer, nor to proceedings before an arbitrator.
(3) It shall come into force on such date as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint.

breakdown.plain_summary: This opening section names the Act, fixes what kinds of proceedings it governs, and leaves its start date to be announced later by the Central Government. It applies broadly to judicial proceedings before any Court, including Courts-martial, but pointedly excludes affidavits and arbitration proceedings -- both of which follow their own, more relaxed evidentiary norms.
essential_elements: Subsection (1) names the Act the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023.
Subsection (2) applies it to all judicial proceedings in or before any Court, expressly including Courts-martial.
Subsection (2) excludes affidavits presented to any Court or officer, and proceedings before an arbitrator, from the Act's application.
Subsection (3) leaves the commencement date to a Central Government notification in the Official Gazette.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Affidavits are outside the Adhiniyam's scope even though they are sworn statements used in judicial proceedings -- their admissibility and form are governed by procedural law, not by this evidence code.
Arbitration proceedings are also excluded, consistent with arbitration's traditional freedom from the strict rules of evidence that bind ordinary courts.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the BSA's replacement for the old Indian Evidence Act, 1872's section 1 -- functionally identical in scope (Courts-martial included, affidavits and arbitration excluded), confirming continuity in what the new evidence code does and does not cover.

sections.title: Definitions

breakdown.plain_summary: This dense interpretation clause is the conceptual foundation for the entire Adhiniyam. Its most important work is defining a graduated vocabulary for how confident the Court must be about a fact: 'proved' and 'disproved' set the basic standard (a prudent person acting on the probability), 'not proved' captures genuine uncertainty, and 'may presume' / 'shall presume' / 'conclusive proof' describe three increasingly strict presumption rules the Adhiniyam uses elsewhere. It also defines 'Court', 'document' (expressly including electronic and digital records), 'evidence' (oral and documentary, including electronic statements), 'fact', and 'facts in issue' -- and subsection (2) borrows definitions from the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the sister BNSS/BNS codes for any term used but not separately defined here.
essential_elements: “Court” includes all Judges and Magistrates and any person legally authorised to take evidence, but excludes arbitrators.
“Conclusive proof”: once the foundational fact is proved, the Court must treat the declared fact as proved and no evidence to disprove it is admissible.
“Document” covers any matter recorded on any substance by any means intended for recording, and expressly includes electronic and digital records.

“Evidence” includes both oral evidence (statements, including electronic statements, made before the Court) and documentary evidence (documents, including electronic/digital records, produced for inspection).
“Fact” includes both physical things/states/relations perceivable by the senses and mental conditions a person is conscious of.
“Facts in issue” are the facts from which the existence, non-existence, nature or extent of an asserted or denied right, liability or disability necessarily follows.
“May presume” gives the Court discretion to treat a fact as proved unless disproved, or to instead call for proof.
“Shall presume” requires the Court to treat a fact as proved unless and until disproved -- no discretion, but rebuttable.
“Proved” / “disproved” / “not proved” set the basic belief/probability standard courts apply to every factual finding.
“Relevant” means connected to another fact in one of the specific ways the Adhiniyam's relevancy provisions describe.
Subsection (2) imports definitions from the Information Technology Act, 2000, the BNSS, and the BNS for undefined terms used in this Adhiniyam.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Arbitrators are expressly excluded from the definition of “Court” even though they perform an evidence-taking function, consistent with section 1(2) excluding arbitration proceedings from the Adhiniyam's scope altogether.
breakdown.how_to_read: This section is the master glossary for the whole Adhiniyam -- whenever a later section uses 'shall presume', 'conclusive proof', or 'may presume', the precise legal consequence is fixed here, not by ordinary English usage; misreading which of the three presumption tiers applies to a given provision is a common source of error in evidence-law argument.

sections.title: Evidence may be given of facts in issue and relevant facts
sections.raw_text:
3. Evidence may be given in any suit or proceeding of the existence or non-existence of every fact in issue and of such other facts as are hereinafter declared to be relevant, and of no others.
Explanation.—This section shall not enable any person to give evidence of a fact which he is disentitled to prove by any provision of the law for the time being in force relating to civil procedure.
Illustrations.
(a) A is tried for the murder of B by beating him with a club with the intention of causing his death.
At A's trial the following facts are in issue:—
A's beating B with the club;
A's causing B's death by such beating;
A's intention to cause B's death.
(b) A suitor does not bring with him, and have in readiness for production at the first hearing of the case, a bond on which he relies. This section does not enable him to produce the bond or prove its contents at a subsequent stage of the proceedings, otherwise than in accordance with the conditions prescribed by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the Adhiniyam's foundational gatekeeping rule: evidence may only be given of facts in issue and of facts the Adhiniyam elsewhere declares relevant -- nothing else. It is both permissive (facts in issue and relevant facts CAN be proved) and restrictive (facts that are neither in issue nor declared relevant CANNOT be proved through evidence), making it the entry point for every relevancy analysis that follows in Chapter II.
essential_elements: Evidence may be given of the existence or non-existence of every fact in issue.
Evidence may also be given of facts the Adhiniyam elsewhere declares to be relevant.
Evidence may be given of no facts other than these two categories.
The Explanation clarifies this section does not override separate civil procedure rules that may disentitle a person from proving a fact (e.g., for failing to produce a document when required).
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Explanation is a carve-out: even if a fact is technically a fact in issue or relevant, a person may still be barred from proving it by a specific civil procedure rule (illustration (b)'s example of failing to produce a bond in time).
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the threshold question in every evidentiary dispute: before asking whether evidence is admissible under a specific rule, first ask whether the fact it proves is a fact in issue or has been declared relevant by some provision later in this Chapter -- if neither, section 3 bars it outright regardless of how probative it might seem.

sections.title: Relevancy of facts forming part of same transaction
sections.raw_text:
4. Facts which, though not in issue, are so connected with a fact in issue or a relevant fact as to form part of the same transaction, are relevant, whether they occurred at the same time and place or at different times and places.
Illustrations.
(a) A is accused of the murder of B by beating him. Whatever was said or done by A or B or the bystanders at the beating, or so shortly before or after it as to form part of the transaction, is a relevant fact.
(b) A is accused of waging war against the Government of India by taking part in an armed insurrection in which property is destroyed, troops are attacked and jails are broken open. The occurrence of these facts is relevant, as forming part of the general transaction, though A may not have been present at all of them.
(c) A sues B for a libel contained in a letter forming part of a correspondence. Letters between the parties relating to the subject out of which the libel arose, and forming part of the correspondence in which it is contained, are relevant facts, though they do not contain the libel itself.
(d) The question is, whether certain goods ordered from B were delivered to A. The goods were delivered to several intermediate persons successively. Each delivery is a relevant fact.

breakdown.plain_summary: Known to lawyers by the common-law label 'res gestae', this section makes facts relevant simply because they form part of the same transaction as a fact in issue or another relevant fact -- even if they occurred at a different time or place. The connecting thread is not chronology or geography, but whether the facts are so bound together that understanding one requires understanding the whole transaction.
essential_elements: The fact need not itself be in issue.
It must be so connected with a fact in issue or a relevant fact as to form part of the same transaction.
Such facts are relevant regardless of whether they occurred at the same time and place, or at different times and places.
breakdown.how_to_read: Courts read 'same transaction' as requiring proximity of purpose and continuity of action, not merely topical relatedness -- illustration (a)'s words spoken 'shortly before or after' a beating qualify, but a loosely related event separated by a meaningful break in the action typically would not.

sections.title: Facts which are occasion, cause or effect of facts in issue or relevant facts
sections.raw_text:
5. Facts which are the occasion, cause or effect, immediate or otherwise, of relevant facts, or facts in issue, or which constitute the state of things under which they happened, or which afforded an opportunity for their occurrence or transaction, are relevant.
Illustrations.
(a) The question is, whether A robbed B. The facts that, shortly before the robbery, B went to a fair with money in his possession, and that he showed it, or mentioned the fact that he had it, to third persons, are relevant.
(b) The question is, whether A murdered B. Marks on the ground, produced by a struggle at or near the place where the murder was committed, are relevant facts.
(c) The question is, whether A poisoned B. The state of B's health before the symptoms ascribed to poison, and habits of B, known to A, which afforded an opportunity for the administration of poison, are relevant facts.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section widens relevancy to reach facts that are the occasion, cause, or effect of a fact in issue or relevant fact, the surrounding 'state of things' in which it happened, or facts that afforded the opportunity for it to occur -- essentially, the causal and situational backdrop against which the disputed event took place.
essential_elements: Facts that are the occasion of a relevant fact or fact in issue are relevant.
Facts that are the cause, immediate or otherwise, of a relevant fact or fact in issue are relevant.
Facts that are the effect, immediate or otherwise, of a relevant fact or fact in issue are relevant.
Facts constituting the state of things under which the relevant fact or fact in issue happened are relevant.
Facts affording an opportunity for the occurrence or transaction of a relevant fact or fact in issue are relevant.
breakdown.how_to_read: This provision is frequently invoked to admit circumstantial, scene-setting evidence -- physical marks at a crime scene, a victim's pre-existing condition, or an opportunity the accused had -- none of which directly proves the fact in issue but which situates it causally and factually.

sections.title: Motive, preparation and previous or subsequent conduct
sections.raw_text:
6. (1) Any fact is relevant which shows or constitutes a motive or preparation for any fact in issue or relevant fact.
(2) The conduct of any party, or of any agent to any party, to any suit or proceeding, in reference to such suit or proceeding, or in reference to any fact in issue therein or relevant thereto, and the conduct of any person, an offence against whom is the subject of any proceeding, is relevant, if such conduct influences or is influenced by any fact in issue or relevant fact, and whether it was previous or subsequent thereto.
Explanation 1.—The word “conduct” in this section does not include statements, unless those statements accompany and explain acts other than statements; but this explanation is not to affect the relevancy of statements under any other section of this Adhiniyam.
Explanation 2.—When the conduct of any person is relevant, any statement made to him or in his presence and hearing, which affects such conduct, is relevant.
Illustrations.
(a) A is tried for the murder of B. The facts that A murdered C, that B knew that A had murdered C, and that B had tried to extort money from A by threatening to make his knowledge public, are relevant.
(b) A sues B upon a bond for the payment of money. B denies the making of the bond. The fact that, at the time when the bond was alleged to be made, B required money for a particular purpose, is relevant.
(c) A is tried for the murder of B by poison. The fact that, before the death of B, A procured poison similar to that which was administered to B, is relevant.
(d) The question is, whether a certain document is the will of A. The facts that, not long before, the date of the alleged will, A made inquiry into matters to which the provisions of the alleged will relate; that he consulted advocates in reference to making the will, and that he caused drafts of other wills to be prepared, of which he did not approve, are relevant.
(e) A is accused of a crime. The facts that, either before, or at the time of, or after the alleged crime, A provided evidence which would tend to give to the facts of the case an appearance favourable to himself, or that he destroyed or concealed evidence, or prevented the presence or procured the absence of persons who might have been witnesses, or suborned persons to give false evidence respecting it, are relevant.
(f) The question is, whether A robbed B. The facts that, after B was robbed, C said in A's presence—“the police are coming to look for the person who robbed B”, and that immediately afterwards A ran away, are relevant.
(g) The question is, whether A owes B ten thousand rupees. The facts that A asked C to lend him money, and that D said to C in A's presence and hearing—“I advise you not to trust A, for he owes B ten thousand rupees”, and that A went away without making any answer, are relevant facts.
(h) The question is, whether A committed a crime. The fact that A absconded, after receiving a letter, warning A that inquiry was being made for the criminal, and the contents of the letter, are relevant.
(i) A is accused of a crime. The facts that, after the commission of the alleged crime, A absconded, or was in possession of property or the proceeds of property acquired by the crime, or attempted to conceal things which were or might have been used in committing it, are relevant.
(j) The question is, whether A was raped. The fact that, shortly after the alleged rape, A made a complaint relating to the crime, the circumstances under which, and the terms in which, the complaint was made, are relevant. The fact that, without making a complaint, A said that A had been raped is not relevant as conduct under this section, though it may be relevant as a dying declaration under clause (a) of section 26, or as corroborative evidence under section 160.
(k) The question is, whether A was robbed. The fact that, soon after the alleged robbery, A made a complaint relating to the offence, the circumstances under which, and the terms in which, the complaint was made, are relevant. The fact that A said he had been robbed, without making any complaint, is not relevant, as conduct under this section, though it may be relevant as a dying declaration under clause (a) of section 26, or as corroborative evidence under section 160.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is one of the most heavily litigated relevancy provisions. Subsection (1) makes motive and preparation relevant to any fact in issue. Subsection (2) makes a party's or accused's conduct relevant, before or after the events in question, so long as it influences or is influenced by a fact in issue or relevant fact -- covering things like absconding, destroying evidence, or making (or conspicuously not making) a complaint. Explanation 1 draws a sharp line: mere statements are not 'conduct' unless they accompany and explain a non-verbal act, though they may still be relevant under other sections. Explanation 2 makes a statement made to, or in the presence and hearing of, a person whose conduct is relevant, itself relevant -- because it helps explain that conduct.
essential_elements: Subsection (1): facts showing or constituting motive or preparation for a fact in issue or relevant fact are relevant.

Subsection (2): the conduct of a party, a party's agent, or the person accused/affected, is relevant if it influences or is influenced by a fact in issue or relevant fact -- whether previous or subsequent.
Explanation 1: 'conduct' excludes bare statements unless they accompany and explain a non-verbal act -- but this does not stop those statements being relevant under some other section.
Explanation 2: where a person's conduct is relevant, statements made to that person, or in their presence and hearing, that affect the conduct, are themselves relevant.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Illustrations (j) and (k) draw a critical distinction: silently claiming to have been raped or robbed, without any accompanying complaint, is not relevant conduct under this section -- though it may still be admissible as a dying declaration under section 26(a) or as corroborative evidence under section 160.
breakdown.how_to_read: When arguing relevance of an accused's behaviour (fleeing, hiding evidence, staying silent, making a prompt complaint), classify it carefully: is it 'conduct' proper (subsection (2)), or is it really a 'statement' masquerading as conduct that Explanation 1 excludes unless it explains a physical act -- the prompt-complaint illustrations (j) and (k) show how easily the two get confused in practice.

sections.title: Facts necessary to explain or introduce fact in issue or relevant facts
sections.raw_text:
7. Facts necessary to explain or introduce a fact in issue or relevant fact, or which support or rebut an inference suggested by a fact in issue or a relevant fact, or which establish the identity of anything, or person whose identity, is relevant, or fix the time or place at which any fact in issue or relevant fact happened, or which show the relation of parties by whom any such fact was transacted, are relevant in so far as they are necessary for that purpose.
Illustrations.
(a) The question is, whether a given document is the will of A. The state of A's property and of his family at the date of the alleged will may be relevant facts.
(b) A sues B for a libel imputing disgraceful conduct to A; B affirms that the matter alleged to be libellous is true. The position and relations of the parties at the time when the libel was published may be relevant facts as introductory to the facts in issue. The particulars of a dispute between A and B about a matter unconnected with the alleged libel are irrelevant, though the fact that there was a dispute may be relevant if it affected the relations between A and B.
(c) A is accused of a crime. The fact that, soon after the commission of the crime, A absconded from his house, is relevant under section 6, as conduct subsequent to and affected by facts in issue. The fact that, at the time when he left home, A had sudden and urgent business at the place to which he went, is relevant, as tending to explain the fact that he left home suddenly. The details of the business on which he left are not relevant, except in so far as they are necessary to show that the business was sudden and urgent.
(d) A sues B for inducing C to break a contract of service made by him with A. C, on leaving A's service, says to A—“I am leaving you because B has made me a better offer”. This statement is a relevant fact as explanatory of C's conduct, which is relevant as a fact in issue.
(e) A, accused of theft, is seen to give the stolen property to B, who is seen to give it to A's wife. B says as he delivers it—“A says you are to hide this”. B's statement is relevant as explanatory of a fact which is part of the transaction.
(f) A is tried for a riot and is proved to have marched at the head of a mob. The cries of the mob are relevant as explanatory of the nature of the transaction.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section admits facts needed to explain, introduce, fix the time/place of, establish the identity connected with, or show the relations of the parties to, a fact in issue or relevant fact -- but only to the extent necessary for that explanatory purpose. It is a purpose-limited relevancy rule: the facts themselves may otherwise seem tangential, but they are admitted strictly to make sense of the facts in issue, not for their own sake.
essential_elements: Facts necessary to explain or introduce a fact in issue or relevant fact are relevant.
Facts that support or rebut an inference suggested by a fact in issue or relevant fact are relevant.
Facts establishing the identity of anything or any person whose identity is relevant are covered.
Facts fixing the time or place at which a fact in issue or relevant fact happened are covered.
Facts showing the relation of the parties by whom a relevant transaction was carried out are covered.
In every case, such facts are relevant only in so far as necessary for the explanatory purpose -- not without limit.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Illustration (c) shows the necessity limit in action: that the accused had urgent business is relevant to explain why he left suddenly, but the details of that business are not relevant beyond what is needed to show it was sudden and urgent.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a 'connective tissue' relevancy rule -- it does not independently prove guilt or liability the way sections 4-6 do, but supplies the explanatory context (identity, timing, relationships, rebutting inferences) that makes the core facts in issue intelligible to the Court.

sections.title: Things said or done by conspirator in reference to common design
sections.raw_text:
8. Where there is reasonable ground to believe that two or more persons have conspired together to commit an offence or an actionable wrong, anything said, done or written by any one of such persons in reference to their common intention, after the time when such intention was first entertained by any one of them, is a relevant fact as against each of the persons believed to be so conspiring, as well for the purpose of proving the existence of the conspiracy as for the purpose of showing that any such person was a party to it.
Illustration.
Reasonable ground exists for believing that A has joined in a conspiracy to wage war against the State.
The facts that B procured arms in Europe for the purpose of the conspiracy, C collected money in Kolkata for a like object, D persuaded persons to join the conspiracy in Mumbai, E published writings advocating the object in view at Agra, and F transmitted from Delhi to G at Singapore the money which C had collected at Kolkata, and the contents of a letter written by H giving an account of the conspiracy, are each relevant, both to prove the existence of the conspiracy, and to prove A's complicity in it, although he may have been ignorant of all of them, and although the persons by whom they were done were strangers to him, and although they may have taken place before he joined the conspiracy or after he left it.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section lets what one conspirator said, did, or wrote in furtherance of a shared criminal or wrongful plan be used as evidence against every other member of the conspiracy -- even members who never met, never knew of that particular act, or joined the conspiracy after it happened. The only threshold requirement is 'reasonable ground to believe' a conspiracy exists in the first place.
essential_elements: There must be reasonable ground to believe two or more persons conspired to commit an offence or an actionable wrong.
The statement, act, or writing must be by one of the conspirators, in reference to their common intention.
It must be after the time the common intention was first entertained by any one of them.
It is then relevant against each person believed to be a conspirator, both to prove the conspiracy exists and to prove that particular person's membership in it.
Per the illustration, this holds even if the person against whom it is used was ignorant of the act, a stranger to the person who did it, or joined/left the conspiracy before/after it occurred.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the evidentiary backbone of conspiracy prosecutions: it is what allows the prosecution to weave together acts of different co-conspirators, done in different places and even at different times relative to when a particular defendant joined, into a single case against each member -- but the 'reasonable ground to believe a conspiracy exists' threshold must be independently established first, usually from other evidence, before this section's expanded relevancy rule can be invoked.

sections.title: When facts not otherwise relevant become relevant
sections.raw_text:
9. Facts not otherwise relevant are relevant—
(1) if they are inconsistent with any fact in issue or relevant fact;
(2) if by themselves or in connection with other facts they make the existence or non-existence of any fact in issue or relevant fact highly probable or improbable.
Illustrations.
(a) The question is, whether A committed a crime at Chennai on a certain day. The fact that, on that day, A was at Ladakh is relevant. The fact that, near the time when the crime was committed, A was at a distance from the place where it was committed, which would render it highly improbable, though not impossible, that he committed it, is relevant.
(b) The question is, whether A committed a crime. The circumstances are such that the crime must have been committed either by A, B, C or D. Every fact which shows that the crime could have been committed by no one else, and that it was not committed by either B, C or D, is relevant.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the Adhiniyam's version of the classic 'alibi' provision: facts that would otherwise have no relevancy connection at all become relevant if they are inconsistent with a fact in issue (like being provably elsewhere when a crime occurred), or if they make a fact in issue highly probable or improbable -- including by process of elimination among a fixed set of suspects.
essential_elements: Clause (1): facts inconsistent with a fact in issue or relevant fact are relevant.
Clause (2): facts that, alone or combined with other facts, make a fact in issue or relevant fact highly probable or improbable are relevant.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The standard is 'highly probable or improbable', not merely somewhat more or less likely -- a weak logical connection is not enough to trigger this section.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the statutory basis for alibi evidence and elimination-style reasoning (illustration (b)'s closed set of possible perpetrators) -- both work by showing the fact in issue is either inconsistent with, or rendered highly improbable by, some other independently established fact.

sections.title: Facts tending to enable Court to determine amount are relevant in suits for damages
sections.raw_text: 10. In suits in which damages are claimed, any fact which will enable the Court to determine the amount of damages which ought to be awarded, is relevant.

breakdown.plain_summary: In a suit claiming damages, any fact that helps the Court fix the correct amount to award is relevant -- a broad, purpose-driven relevancy rule specific to the damages-quantification stage of civil litigation.
essential_elements: The suit must be one in which damages are claimed.
The fact must tend to enable the Court to determine the amount of damages that ought to be awarded.
breakdown.how_to_read: This section works alongside (not instead of) the liability-focused relevancy rules elsewhere in the Chapter -- facts irrelevant to whether the defendant is liable at all may still be relevant here, purely for quantifying what is owed once liability is established.

sections.title: Facts relevant when right or custom is in question
sections.raw_text:
11. Where the question is as to the existence of any right or custom, the following facts are relevant—
(a) any transaction by which the right or custom in question was created, claimed, modified, recognised, asserted or denied, or which was inconsistent with its existence;
(b) particular instances in which the right or custom was claimed, recognised or exercised, or in which its exercise was disputed, asserted or departed from.
Illustration.
The question is, whether A has a right to a fishery. A deed conferring the fishery on A's ancestors, a mortgage of the fishery by A's father, a subsequent grant of the fishery by A's father, irreconcilable with the mortgage, particular instances in which A's father exercised the right, or in which the exercise of the right was stopped by A's neighbours, are relevant facts.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where a case turns on whether a claimed right or custom exists, two categories of facts become relevant: the transactions by which that right or custom was created, claimed, modified, recognised, asserted, denied, or contradicted; and specific instances in which it was actually claimed, recognised, exercised, disputed, or departed from in practice.
essential_elements: The question in the case must be as to the existence of a right or custom.
Clause (a): transactions creating, claiming, modifying, recognising, asserting, or denying the right or custom -- or inconsistent with its existence -- are relevant.
Clause (b): particular instances where the right or custom was claimed, recognised, or exercised, or where its exercise was disputed, asserted, or departed from, are relevant.
breakdown.how_to_read: This section is the evidentiary tool for proving rights of way, easements, fishery and grazing rights, and customary practices -- both the documentary paper trail (deeds, grants, mortgages) and the practical pattern of actual exercise (or challenge to exercise) of the right are independently admissible.

sections.title: Facts showing existence of state of mind, or of body or bodily feeling
sections.raw_text:
12. Facts showing the existence of any state of mind, such as intention, knowledge, good faith, negligence, rashness, ill-will or goodwill towards any particular person, or showing the existence of any state of body or bodily feeling, are relevant, when the existence of any such state of mind or body or bodily feeling is in issue or relevant.
Explanation 1.—A fact relevant as showing the existence of a relevant state of mind must show that the state of mind exists, not generally, but in reference to the particular matter in question.
Explanation 2.—But where, upon the trial of a person accused of an offence, the previous commission by the accused of an offence is relevant within the meaning of this section, the previous conviction of such person shall also be a relevant fact.
Illustrations.
(a) A is accused of receiving stolen goods knowing them to be stolen. It is proved that he was in possession of a particular stolen article. The fact that, at the same time, he was in possession of many other stolen articles is relevant, as tending to show that he knew each and all of the articles of which he was in possession to be stolen.
(b) A is accused of fraudulently delivering to another person a counterfeit currency which, at the time when he delivered it, he knew to be counterfeit. The fact that, at the time of its delivery, A was possessed of a number of other pieces of counterfeit currency is relevant. The fact that A had been previously convicted of delivering to another person as genuine a counterfeit currency knowing it to be counterfeit is relevant.
(c) A sues B for damage done by a dog of B's, which B knew to be ferocious. The fact that the dog had previously bitten X, Y and Z, and that they had made complaints to B, are relevant.
(d) The question is, whether A, the acceptor of a bill of exchange, knew that the name of the payee was fictitious. The fact that A had accepted other bills drawn in the same manner before they could have been transmitted to him by the payee if the payee had been a real person, is relevant, as showing that A knew that the payee was a fictitious person.
(e) A is accused of defaming B by publishing an imputation intended to harm the reputation of B. The fact of previous publications by A respecting B, showing ill-will on the part of A towards B is relevant, as proving A's intention to harm B's reputation by the particular publication in question. The facts that there was no previous quarrel between A and B, and that A repeated the matter complained of as he heard it, are relevant, as showing that A did not intend to harm the reputation of B.
(f) A is sued by B for fraudulently representing to B that C was solvent, whereby B, being induced to trust C, who was insolvent, suffered loss. The fact that, at the time when A represented C to be solvent, C was supposed to be solvent by his neighbours and by persons dealing with him, is relevant, as showing that A made the representation in good faith.
(g) A is sued by B for the price of work done by B, upon a house of which A is owner, by the order of C, a contractor. A's defence is that B's contract was with C. The fact that A paid C for the work in question is relevant, as proving that A did, in good faith, make over to C the management of the work in question, so that C was in a position to contract with B on C's own account, and not as agent for A.
(h) A is accused of the dishonest misappropriation of property which he had found, and the question is whether, when he appropriated it, he believed in good faith that the real owner could not be found. The fact that public notice of the loss of the property had been given in the place where A was, is relevant, as showing that A did not in good faith believe that the real owner of the property could not be found. The fact that A knew, or had reason to believe, that the notice was given fraudulently by C, who had heard of the loss of the property and wished to set up a false claim to it, is relevant, as showing that the fact that A knew of the notice did not disprove A's good faith.
(i) A is charged with shooting at B with intent to kill him. In order to show A's intent, the fact of A's having previously shot at B may be proved.
(j) A is charged with sending threatening letters to B. Threatening letters previously sent by A to B may be proved, as showing the intention of the letters.
(k) The question is, whether A has been guilty of cruelty towards B, his wife. Expressions of their feeling towards each other shortly before or after the alleged cruelty are relevant facts.
(l) The question is, whether A's death was caused by poison. Statements made by A during his illness as to his symptoms are relevant facts.
(m) The question is, what was the state of A's health at the time when an assurance on his life was effected. Statements made by A as to the state of his health at or near the time in question are relevant facts.
(n) A sues B for negligence in providing him with a car for hire not reasonably fit for use, whereby A was injured. The fact that B's attention was drawn on other occasions to the defect of that particular car is relevant. The fact that B was habitually negligent about the cars which he let to hire is irrelevant.
(o) A is tried for the murder of B by intentionally shooting him dead. The fact that A on other occasions shot at B is relevant as showing his intention to shoot B. The fact that A was in the habit of shooting at people with intent to murder them is irrelevant.
(p) A is tried for a crime. The fact that he said something indicating an intention to commit that particular crime is relevant. The fact that he said something indicating a general disposition to commit crimes of that class is irrelevant.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section admits facts showing a person's state of mind (intention, knowledge, good faith, negligence, rashness, ill-will, goodwill) or state of body/bodily feeling, wherever that mental or physical state is itself in issue or relevant. Explanation 1 is the critical limiting principle: the state of mind shown must relate specifically to the matter in question -- not be evidence of a general character trait or disposition. Explanation 2 carves out one exception: where a prior offence is relevant under this section to show state of mind, the prior conviction for it is also relevant.
essential_elements: Facts showing intention, knowledge, good faith, negligence, rashness, ill-will, or goodwill are relevant when that state of mind is in issue or relevant.
Facts showing a state of body or bodily feeling are relevant on the same basis.
Explanation 1: the state of mind must be shown in reference to the particular matter in question, not as a general character trait.
Explanation 2: where a prior offence becomes relevant under this section, the previous conviction for it is also a relevant fact.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Illustrations (o) and (p) draw the crucial line this section polices: specific prior acts directed at the same target, or a specific stated intention to commit the particular crime charged, are relevant -- but a general habit or general disposition to commit that class of crime is irrelevant.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the codified boundary between admissible 'specific intent/knowledge' evidence and inadmissible 'propensity' or bad-character evidence -- Explanation 1 and illustrations (o)/(p) together are the standard authority cited whenever a party tries to introduce a pattern of similar past conduct to prove state of mind in the present case.

sections.title: Facts bearing on question whether act was accidental or intentional
sections.raw_text:
13. When there is a question whether an act was accidental or intentional, or done with a particular knowledge or intention, the fact that such act formed part of a series of similar occurrences, in each of which the person doing the act was concerned, is relevant.
Illustrations.
(a) A is accused of burning down his house in order to obtain money for which it is insured. The facts that A lived in several houses successively each of which he insured, in each of which a fire occurred, and after each of which fires A received payment from a different insurance company, are relevant, as tending to show that the fires were not accidental.
(b) A is employed to receive money from the debtors of B. It is A's duty to make entries in a book showing the amounts received by him. He makes an entry showing that on a particular occasion he received less than he really did receive. The question is, whether this false entry was accidental or intentional. The facts that other entries made by A in the same book are false, and that the false entry is in each case in favour of A, are relevant.
(c) A is accused of fraudulently delivering to B a counterfeit currency. The question is, whether the delivery of the currency was accidental. The facts that, soon before or soon after the delivery to B, A delivered counterfeit currency to C, D and E are relevant, as showing that the delivery to B was not accidental.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the 'doctrine of chances' provision: when it is disputed whether an act was accidental or intentional (or done with particular knowledge/intention), the fact that the same person was involved in a series of similar occurrences becomes relevant -- the improbability of the same 'accident' repeatedly happening to the same person tends to show it was not accidental at all.
essential_elements: There must be a question whether the act was accidental or intentional, or done with particular knowledge or intention.
The fact relied on is that the act formed part of a series of similar occurrences.
The same person must have been concerned in each occurrence in the series.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a close cousin of section 12 but analytically distinct: section 12 asks whether prior acts show a state of mind directed at the specific matter in question, while section 13 asks whether the sheer repetition of a similar occurrence to the same person makes 'accident' an implausible explanation -- both often arise together on the same facts (as in illustration (a)'s repeated-fire scenario).

sections.title: Existence of course of business when relevant
sections.raw_text:
14. When there is a question whether a particular act was done, the existence of any course of business, according to which it naturally would have been done, is a relevant fact.
Illustrations.
(a) The question is, whether a particular letter was dispatched. The facts that it was the ordinary course of business for all letters put in a certain place to be carried to the post, and that particular letter was put in that place are relevant.
(b) The question is, whether a particular letter reached A. The facts that it was posted in due course, and was not returned through the Return Letter Office, are relevant.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where the question is whether a particular act was actually done, evidence of a routine, established course of business according to which that act would naturally have occurred is relevant -- letting the Court infer that the usual practice was followed in the specific instance, absent evidence to the contrary.
essential_elements: There must be a question whether a particular act was done.
The relevant fact is the existence of a course of business according to which the act naturally would have been done.
breakdown.how_to_read: This section underlies routine 'presumption of regularity' arguments -- proof of a standing office practice (like a mailroom routine) supports an inference that the specific act in question followed that same routine, without needing direct testimony about that one instance.
